questions.question_text: $\$20\,000$ is invested for $3$ years at $4\%$ p.a. How much more interest does an account compounding annually earn than one paying simple interest, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Gave the compound interest earned rather than the difference between the two accounts.
Gave the simple interest earned rather than the difference between the two accounts.
Gave the compound account's final balance instead of the extra interest earned.

questions.question_text: $\$5000$ is invested for $1$ year, one account at $6\%$ p.a. simple interest and one at $6\%$ p.a. compounding annually. How much more does the compound account hold at the end of the year?

options.why: Gave the interest earned rather than the difference between the two balances.
Charged a second round of interest on the first year's $\$300$, which has not been earned yet.
Gave the compound account's balance instead of the difference between the accounts.

questions.question_text: Bank X pays $8\%$ p.a. simple interest. Bank Y pays $6.8\%$ p.a. compounding annually. $\$7000$ is invested for $4$ years. Which bank gives the greater final balance, and by how much, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Assumed compound interest always wins, so named the wrong bank for the correct difference.
Worked out Bank Y with $I=Prn$ as well, treating its compound rate as a simple rate.
Compounded Bank X's $8\%$ as well, comparing $\$9523.42$ with $\$9107.16$.

options.text: $A$ pays compound interest, because its balance rises by a larger amount each year.
$B$ pays compound interest, because its graph is a straight line.
options.why: A straight line means the same interest is added each year, which is simple interest.

options.text: $A$ pays compound interest, because it started with a larger deposit.
options.why: Both graphs start at the same balance; the curve comes from the growing yearly interest.

options.text: $B$ pays compound interest, because it is above $A$ in the early years.
options.why: The two balances are equal after one year, so neither graph is above the other early on.

questions.solution_text:
Graph $B$ is a straight line, so the same amount of interest is added each year: that is simple interest.
Graph $A$ curves upwards, so each year's interest is larger than the year before: that is compound interest.

options.why: At year $5$ Offer Q holds $\$4306.89$ against $\$4350$, so it is still $\$43.11$ behind.
Went one year past the first year in which Offer Q moves ahead.
Assumed compound interest is ahead immediately, but the balances are equal after one year.

questions.solution_text:
Offer P: $3000+270n$
Offer Q: $3000(1.075)^{n}$
$n=5$: $\$4350$ and $\$4306.89$, so P is ahead.
$n=6$: $\$4620$ and $\$4629.90$, so Q is ahead.
Offer Q first moves ahead in year $6$.

questions.question_text: $\$10\,000$ is invested at $7\%$ p.a., once as simple interest and once compounding annually. After $2$ years the compound account is $\$49.00$ ahead. How far ahead is it after $4$ years, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Doubled the two-year gap, assuming the gap grows by the same amount each year.
Gave the compound interest earned over $4$ years instead of the gap between the accounts.
Gave the simple interest earned over $4$ years instead of the gap between the accounts.

questions.question_text:
The table shows the balance of two accounts, each opened with $\$6000$ at $9\%$ p.a. One pays simple interest and the other compounds annually.

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}\text{Year}&1&2&3\\\hline \text{Account P}&\$6540&\$7080&\$7620\\\hline \text{Account Q}&\$6540&\$7128.60&\$7770.17\end{array}$

Which account pays simple interest, and how can you tell?

options.text: Account P, because its balance rises by $\$540$ every year.
Account Q, because its balance rises by a larger amount each year.
options.why: A rise that grows each year is interest paid on interest, which is compound interest.

options.text: Account P, because it has the smaller balance after $3$ years.
options.why: The smaller balance is a result of simple interest, not the test; the test is a constant yearly rise.

options.text: Account Q, because both accounts hold the same amount after $1$ year.
options.why: Equal balances after one year happen for both interest types, so this identifies neither.

questions.solution_text:
Account P rises by $\$540$, then $\$540$, then $\$540$: a constant amount each year.
Account Q rises by $\$540$, then $\$588.60$, then $\$641.57$: a growing amount each year.
Account P pays simple interest, because the same interest is added every year.

questions.question_text: $\$8000$ is invested at $5.5\%$ p.a. compounding annually for $8$ years. What simple interest rate would earn the same total interest over those $8$ years, correct to $2$ decimal places?

options.why: Assumed the equivalent simple rate is just the compound rate, so no calculation was done.
Left $n$ out of $I=Prn$, dividing the interest by the principal alone.
Used the future value instead of the interest earned as $I$ in $I=Prn$.

questions.solution_text:
$FV = 8000(1.055)^{8}$
$=\$12\,277.49$
Compound interest $=12\,277.49-8000=\$4277.49$
$I = Prn$
$4277.4884\ldots=8000\times r\times8$
$r=0.066835\ldots$
The equivalent simple interest rate is $6.68\%$ p.a.

questions.question_text: Offer A pays $10\%$ p.a. simple interest and Offer B pays $8\%$ p.a. compounding annually, on a deposit of $\$8000$. In which year does Offer B first move ahead of Offer A, and by how much is it ahead at that time, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Took the last year in which Offer B is still behind, and gave the size of that shortfall.
Gave Offer B's balance in that year instead of the amount by which it is ahead.
Went one year past the first year in which Offer B moves ahead.
